statement: For $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$, the assignment $\rho \mapsto \pi(\rho)$ is a bijection from isomorphism classes of irreducible two-dimensional continuous [Galois representations](c:galois-representation) $\rho$ of $G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ onto isomorphism classes of supersingular irreducible smooth [mod p representations](c:mod-p-representation) of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$.

hypotheses.text: The group is $\mathrm{GL}_2$, the local field is $\mathbb{Q}_p$ itself, and the coefficients lie in $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$.
The representation $\rho\colon G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}\to\mathrm{GL}_2(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ is continuous and [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation).

conclusion: Each such $\rho$ gives exactly one supersingular $\pi(\rho)$, and each supersingular representation comes from exactly one $\rho$.

proofs.name: Breuil's classification of supersingular representations
proofs.slogan: Match the supersingular representations of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ with the irreducible two-dimensional Galois representations through their common list of parameters.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof for $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ and irreducible $\rho$. Reducible $\rho$ (principal series), Colmez's functor and the link with the $p$-adic correspondence are not covered, and no other group or base field has a known correspondence.

roles.why: Only for $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ is the Hecke algebra of the maximal compact subgroup simple enough to list every supersingular representation.
[Irreducibility](c:irreducible-representation) of $\rho$ gives the form induced from the unramified quadratic extension, which matches the supersingular parameters.

steps.slogan: List the supersingular representations as quotients of compact inductions.
steps.detail: Every supersingular representation is a quotient of $\mathrm{c\text{-}Ind}_{KZ}^{G}\,\mathrm{Sym}^r\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^2$ by the Hecke operator $T$, twisted by a character (Barthel and Livné). Breuil proves that each quotient $\pi(r,0,\chi)$ with $0\le r\le p-1$ is irreducible.

steps.slogan: Determine which of the representations $\pi(r,0,\chi)$ are isomorphic.
steps.detail: Breuil shows by an explicit study of the compact induction that $\pi(r,0,\chi)\cong\pi(r,0,\chi\mu_{-1})\cong\pi(p-1-r,0,\chi\omega^r)\cong\pi(p-1-r,0,\chi\omega^r\mu_{-1})$, with $\mu_{-1}$ the unramified quadratic character. There are no other isomorphisms.

steps.slogan: List the irreducible two-dimensional representations of $G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$.
steps.detail: Such a $\rho$ is $\mathrm{ind}(\omega_2^{r+1})\otimes\chi$ with $0\le r\le p-1$ and $\chi$ a character, where $\mathrm{ind}$ is induction from the unramified quadratic extension. Two parameters give isomorphic $\rho$ exactly under the same four identifications: the twist by $\mu_{-1}$ is absorbed by the induction, and $\omega_2^{p}$ is the Galois conjugate of $\omega_2$ with $\omega_2^{p+1}=\omega$.

steps.slogan: Match the two lists parameter by parameter to get the bijection.
steps.detail: Send $\rho=\mathrm{ind}(\omega_2^{r+1})\otimes\chi$ to $\pi(\rho)=\pi(r,0,\chi)$. Both sides are the set of pairs $(r,\chi)$ modulo the same four identifications, so the map is well defined and bijective.

concepts.c:galois-representation: The Galois side of the correspondence consists of these representations.
concepts.c:mod-p-representation: The group side consists of smooth representations over a field of characteristic $p$.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Irreducibility selects the representations induced from the unramified quadratic extension.

source.ref: C. Breuil, Sur quelques représentations modulaires et p-adiques de GL2(Qp), I, Compositio Mathematica 138 (2003), 165-188
source.note: Breuil lists the supersingular representations and their isomorphisms and matches them with the irreducible two-dimensional Galois representations. It builds on Barthel and Livné (Duke Math. J. 75, 1994); Berger (Asterisque 330, 2010) shows that Colmez's functor realizes the match.

statement: Consider the [singular perturbation](c:singular-perturbation) problem $\varepsilon\dot x = f(x,y)$, $\dot y = g(x,y)$ whose [slow manifold](c:slow-manifold) $x = h(y)$ is uniformly exponentially stable for the frozen fast equation. If $\bar y$ solves $\dot{\bar y} = g(h(\bar y),\bar y)$ on $[0,T]$, then for small $\varepsilon$, $y = \bar y + O(\varepsilon)$ on $[0,T]$ and $x = h(\bar y) + O(\varepsilon)$ on $[t_1,T]$ for each $t_1>0$.

hypotheses.text: The functions $f$, $g$ and $h$ are $C^1$ on a domain that contains the solutions.
The function $h$ satisfies $f(h(y),y)=0$, so $x=h(y)$ is the [slow manifold](c:slow-manifold).
The root $h(y)$ is a uniformly exponentially stable equilibrium of $\dot x=f(x,y)$ for frozen $y$, and $x(0)-h(y(0))$ lies in a compact subset of its region of attraction.
The reduced solution $\bar y$ with $\bar y(0)=y(0)$ exists on $[0,T]$ and stays in a compact set.

conclusion: For small $\varepsilon$, $\|y(t)-\bar y(t)\|=O(\varepsilon)$ on $[0,T]$ and $\|x(t)-h(\bar y(t))\|=O(\varepsilon)$ on $[t_1,T]$.

proofs.name: Lyapunov bound and Gronwall
proofs.slogan: Track the distance of the fast variable to the moving equilibrium by a Lyapunov bound, then compare the slow variable with the reduced solution by Gronwall's inequality.
proofs.scope: A finite interval $[0,T]$ only. The fast variable is close to $h(\bar y)$ after an initial layer of length of order $\varepsilon$, so $t_1>0$ is needed for $x$; the loose phrase 'the variable $x$ is fast' means that $\varepsilon$ is small.

roles.why: Lipschitz bounds on $f$, $g$ and $h'$ control the terms of the equations for $z$ and $y$.
The root $h$ defines the moving equilibrium that the shift subtracts, on the [slow manifold](c:slow-manifold).
Uniform exponential stability gives a [Lyapunov function](c:lyapunov-function) with bounds that do not depend on $y$.
The reduced solution is the comparison curve for $y$ in the Gronwall estimate.

steps.slogan: Shift the fast variable to the moving equilibrium by $z = x - h(y)$.
steps.detail: Differentiating gives $\varepsilon\dot z = f(h(y)+z,y) - \varepsilon\,h'(y)\,g(h(y)+z,y)$. The first term is the frozen fast equation with equilibrium $z=0$, and the second term is of order $\varepsilon$ on compact sets.

steps.slogan: Bound $z$ by a decaying exponential plus a term of order $\varepsilon$.
steps.detail: A converse theorem gives a [Lyapunov function](c:lyapunov-function) $V(y,z)$ with $c_1\|z\|^2\le V\le c_2\|z\|^2$, $\partial_zV\cdot f\le-c_3\|z\|^2$, $\|\partial_zV\|\le c_4\|z\|$ and $\|\partial_yV\|\le c_5\|z\|^2$. For small $\varepsilon$ this gives $\dot V\le-\frac{c_3}{2\varepsilon}\|z\|^2+k\|z\|$, hence $\|z(t)\|\le k_1e^{-at/\varepsilon}+k_2\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Insert the bound on $z$ into the slow equation.
steps.detail: The slow equation reads $\dot y=g(h(y),y)+r(t)$ with $\|r(t)\|\le L\|z(t)\|$, where $L$ is a Lipschitz constant of $g$. Integrating the bound of step 2 gives $\int_0^t\|r\|\,ds\le L(k_1\varepsilon/a+k_2\varepsilon T)=O(\varepsilon)$.

steps.slogan: Compare $y$ with the reduced solution by Grönwall's inequality.
steps.detail: The difference $e=y-\bar y$ satisfies $\|e(t)\|\le\int_0^t\|r\|\,ds+L'\int_0^t\|e\|\,ds$, with $L'$ a Lipschitz constant of $y\mapsto g(h(y),y)$. Grönwall's lemma gives $\|e(t)\|\le O(\varepsilon)e^{L'T}$ on $[0,T]$, and a continuation argument keeps $y$ in the compact set.

steps.slogan: Return to $x$ by combining the estimates for $z$ and $y$.
steps.detail: For $t\ge t_1$ the term $k_1e^{-at/\varepsilon}$ is at most $k_1e^{-at_1/\varepsilon}=O(\varepsilon)$, so $\|z\|=O(\varepsilon)$. Then $\|x-h(\bar y)\|\le\|z\|+\|h(y)-h(\bar y)\|\le O(\varepsilon)+L_h\|y-\bar y\|=O(\varepsilon)$.

concepts.c:singular-perturbation: The small parameter $\varepsilon$ multiplies the derivative of the fast variable.
concepts.c:slow-manifold: The root $x=h(y)$ is the manifold that the fast variable tracks.
concepts.c:lyapunov-function: A Lyapunov function of the frozen fast equation yields the bound on $z$.

source.note: Tikhonov's theorem on a finite interval, as in Khalil, Nonlinear Systems, 3rd edition (Prentice Hall, 2002), Theorem 11.1; this proof keeps only the Lyapunov and Gronwall steps.

statement: For every integer $m\ge1$, every integer $n\ge0$ and every complex $x$, the [Bernoulli polynomials](c:bernoulli-polynomial) satisfy $B_n(mx)=m^{n-1}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}B_n\!\left(x+\tfrac km\right)$.

hypotheses.text: The number $m$ is a positive integer.
The $B_n(x)$ are the [Bernoulli polynomials](c:bernoulli-polynomial), defined by $\frac{t e^{xt}}{e^t-1}=\sum_{n\ge0}B_n(x)\frac{t^n}{n!}$.

conclusion: The identity $B_n(mx)=m^{n-1}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}B_n(x+k/m)$ holds as an identity of polynomials in $x$.

proofs.name: Generating function
proofs.slogan: Compare the generating functions of both sides and sum a geometric series in $e^t$.
proofs.scope: All $n\ge0$ at once, as an identity of power series in $t$ with polynomial coefficients in $x$. This is one member of the family of multiplication theorems; the best known relative is the Gauss formula for the [gamma function](c:gamma-function), which has its own record.

roles.why: The defining generating function gives a closed form for the series at every point $x+k/m$.
An integer $m\ge1$ makes the sum finite and the rescaled series converge on a disc of radius $2\pi/m>0$.

steps.slogan: Write the [generating function](c:generating-function) of $B_n$ at the point $x+k/m$.
steps.detail: By the definition of $B_n$, we have $\sum_{n\ge0}B_n(x+k/m)\,u^n/n!=u\,e^{(x+k/m)u}/(e^u-1)$ for $|u|<2\pi$. This holds for each $k=0,\dots,m-1$.

steps.slogan: Substitute $u=mt$ and divide by $m$ to produce the factor $m^{n-1}$.
steps.detail: Then the series with terms $m^{n-1}B_n(x+k/m)\,t^n/n!$ has the sum $\frac1m\cdot\frac{mt\,e^{(mx+k)t}}{e^{mt}-1}=\frac{t\,e^{mxt}e^{kt}}{e^{mt}-1}$ for $|t|<2\pi/m$.

steps.slogan: Sum over $k$ and evaluate the geometric series $\sum_k e^{kt}$.
steps.detail: Since $\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}e^{kt}=\frac{e^{mt}-1}{e^t-1}$, the sum over $k$ of these series has the sum $\frac{t\,e^{mxt}}{e^{mt}-1}\cdot\frac{e^{mt}-1}{e^t-1}=\frac{t\,e^{mxt}}{e^t-1}$.

steps.slogan: Compare coefficients of $t^n/n!$ with the generating function of $B_n(mx)$.
steps.detail: The last function is $\sum_{n\ge0}B_n(mx)\,t^n/n!$, the generating function at the point $mx$. Two power series that agree near $0$ have equal coefficients, so $B_n(mx)=m^{n-1}\sum_kB_n(x+k/m)$ for every $n$.

concepts.c:bernoulli-polynomial: These polynomials are the objects of the identity.
concepts.c:generating-function: The proof compares generating functions instead of the polynomials.
concepts.c:gamma-function: The best-known multiplication formula is the Gauss formula for the gamma function.

source.note: The standard generating-function proof; the identity is formula 23.1.9 of Abramowitz and Stegun, Handbook of Mathematical Functions.

statement: Let $S$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $g\ge2$ and $G$ a finite subgroup of the [mapping class group](c:mapping-class-group) of $S$. Then $G$ fixes a point of [Teichmüller space](c:teichmuller-space). Equivalently, $G$ is realized by a group of isometries of some [hyperbolic metric](c:hyperbolic-metric) on $S$.

hypotheses.text: The surface $S$ is closed and oriented, of genus $g\ge2$.
The group $G$ is a finite subgroup of the [mapping class group](c:mapping-class-group) $\mathrm{Mod}(S)$.

conclusion: The group $G$ fixes a point of [Teichmüller space](c:teichmuller-space), so $G$ acts by isometries on a [hyperbolic metric](c:hyperbolic-metric) on $S$.

proofs.name: Convexity along earthquake paths
proofs.slogan: Minimize a $G$-invariant proper length function that is strictly convex along earthquake paths, so the unique minimum is fixed by $G$.
proofs.scope: An outline of Kerckhoff's proof for closed surfaces of genus at least 2; punctured, bordered and infinite-type surfaces are not covered. The strict convexity of length functions is cited, not repeated.

roles.why: Genus at least 2 gives hyperbolic metrics, a [Teichmüller space](c:teichmuller-space) with length functions, and the collar lemma.
Finiteness of $G$ makes the orbit of a filling set finite and lets $G$ permute the minima.

steps.slogan: Choose a $G$-invariant finite set $\mathcal A$ of simple closed curves that fill $S$.
steps.detail: Take any finite filling set and replace it by its orbit under the finite group $G$. Then $F(X)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A}\ell_\alpha(X)$ satisfies $F(gX)=F(X)$ for $g\in G$, because $g$ permutes $\mathcal A$.

steps.slogan: Show that the length function $F$ is proper, so that it has a minimum.
steps.detail: If every curve of $\mathcal A$ has length at most $L$, the collar lemma bounds the length of every simple closed curve below, because each such curve crosses $\mathcal A$. Mumford's criterion then gives compactness in moduli space, and only finitely many markings keep the lengths of a filling set below $L$. So $\{F\le L\}$ is compact in [Teichmüller space](c:teichmuller-space), and $F$ attains its minimum.

steps.slogan: Join any two points of Teichmüller space by an earthquake path.
steps.detail: By Thurston's earthquake theorem, for $X\ne Y$ there is a measured lamination $\mu$ with $E_\mu^1X=Y$. The curve $t\mapsto E_\mu^tX$ for $t\in[0,1]$ is an earthquake path from $X$ to $Y$.

steps.slogan: Show that $F$ is strictly convex along every nonconstant earthquake path.
steps.detail: Kerckhoff proves that the length of a closed curve is convex along an earthquake path, and strictly convex when the curve meets the lamination. Since $\mathcal A$ fills $S$, some curve of $\mathcal A$ meets $\mu$, so $F$ is strictly convex.

steps.slogan: Deduce that the minimum of $F$ is unique.
steps.detail: Two minima $X\ne Y$ would be joined by an earthquake path along which $F$ is strictly convex with equal end values equal to the minimum. Then $F$ would be smaller than its minimum in between, which is absurd.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the unique minimum is fixed by $G$ and realizes $G$ by isometries.
steps.detail: The function $F$ is $G$-invariant, so $G$ permutes the set of minima, which has one point $X_0$. A fixed point means that each $g\in G$ is homotopic to an isometry of the [hyperbolic metric](c:hyperbolic-metric) $X_0$. An isometry homotopic to the identity is trivial for $g\ge2$, so $G$ embeds in $\mathrm{Isom}(X_0)$.

concepts.c:mapping-class-group: The group $G$ sits in this group, which acts on Teichmüller space.
concepts.c:teichmuller-space: The fixed point is sought here, where the length functions live.
concepts.c:hyperbolic-metric: A fixed point is a hyperbolic metric whose isometries represent $G$.

source.ref: S. P. Kerckhoff, The Nielsen realization problem, Annals of Mathematics 117 (1983), 235-265
source.note: Kerckhoff combines Thurston's earthquake theorem with his convexity of length functions along earthquake paths. Wolpert (Geodesic length functions and the Nielsen problem, J. Differential Geom. 25, 1987) gives another proof through Weil-Petersson convexity.

statement: Let $\alpha\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$ be a [smooth map](c:smooth-map) with $\alpha(\theta)\to0$ as $|\theta|\to\infty$, the deflection of a bounded transparent lens. For every [regular value](c:regular-value) $\beta$ of the lens map $\eta(\theta)=\theta-\alpha(\theta)$, the equation $\eta(\theta)=\beta$ has finitely many solutions, and their number is odd.

hypotheses.text: The deflection $\alpha$ is a [smooth map](c:smooth-map) of the plane, as for a transparent lens.
The deflection satisfies $\alpha(\theta)\to0$ as $|\theta|\to\infty$, as for a lens of bounded extent.
The source position $\beta$ is a [regular value](c:regular-value) of the lens map $\eta$.

conclusion: The set of images $\eta^{-1}(\beta)$ is finite and has an odd number of points.

proofs.name: Degree of a proper map
proofs.slogan: Deform the lens map to the identity through proper maps, so its degree is 1, and count the preimages of the source modulo 2.
proofs.scope: A regular source only. A source on a caustic (a critical value) is excluded, because its images can merge or be infinite in number.

roles.why: Smoothness lets the inverse function theorem and the [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) of a smooth map apply, and makes $\eta_t$ a smooth homotopy.
Decay of the deflection makes every $\eta_t$ a [proper map](c:proper-map), uniformly in $t$.
A regular value has invertible derivatives at its preimages, so each image counts as $\pm1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the maps $\eta_t(\theta)=\theta-t\alpha(\theta)$ are [proper](c:proper-map) for every $t\in[0,1]$.
steps.detail: Choose $R$ with $|\alpha(\theta)|\le1$ for $|\theta|\ge R$. Then $|\eta_t(\theta)|\ge|\theta|-1$ for $|\theta|\ge R$, so the preimage of a bounded set is bounded and, being closed, compact.

steps.slogan: Show that a regular source has finitely many images.
steps.detail: At a point $\theta$ with $\eta(\theta)=\beta$, the derivative $D\eta(\theta)$ is invertible, so $\theta$ is an isolated point of $\eta^{-1}(\beta)$ by the inverse function theorem. This set is compact by step 1, so it is finite.

steps.slogan: Deform the lens map to the identity and conclude that its degree is 1.
steps.detail: The family $\eta_t$ is a smooth proper homotopy from $\eta_0=\mathrm{id}$ to $\eta_1=\eta$. The [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) of a proper smooth map counts preimages of a regular value with the signs of the Jacobian determinant; regular values exist by Sard's theorem, and the degree is invariant under proper homotopy. So $\deg\eta=\deg\mathrm{id}=1$.

steps.slogan: Count the images with signs to show that their number is odd.
steps.detail: Since $\beta$ is regular, $1=\deg\eta=\sum_{\theta\in\eta^{-1}(\beta)}\operatorname{sign}\det D\eta(\theta)$, a sum of $N$ terms equal to $\pm1$. Such a sum has the same parity as $N$, so $N$ is odd.

concepts.c:smooth-map: Smoothness lets the inverse function theorem and degree theory apply.
concepts.c:regular-value: A regular value has invertible derivatives at its preimages, so the count carries signs.
concepts.c:proper-map: Properness makes preimages compact, so finiteness and degree make sense.
concepts.c:degree-of-a-map: The degree is the homotopy invariant that equals 1 and counts images with signs.

source.note: Degree theory of proper smooth maps of the plane, in the style of Milnor, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint (1965), sections 5 and 6.

statement: For $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ and a finite extension $L$ of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, each absolutely irreducible two-dimensional continuous $L$-[Galois representation](c:galois-representation) $V$ of $G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$ has an associated unitary admissible Banach representation $\Pi(V)$ of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$. The map $V\mapsto\Pi(V)$ is a bijection onto the absolutely irreducible non-ordinary ones, and Colmez's functor recovers $V$ from $\Pi(V)$.

hypotheses.text: The group is $\mathrm{GL}_2$ and the base field is $\mathbb{Q}_p$.
The coefficient field $L$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$.
The representation $V$ is a continuous two-dimensional [p-adic representation](c:p-adic-representation) of $G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$ over $L$ and is absolutely [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation).

conclusion: Each such $V$ gives one non-ordinary $\Pi(V)$, every absolutely irreducible non-ordinary unitary admissible Banach representation arises this way, and $\mathbf V(\Pi(V))\cong V$.

proofs.name: Colmez's construction by (phi,Gamma)-modules
proofs.slogan: Turn $V$ into a $(\varphi,\Gamma)$-module, extend its mirabolic action to a $\mathrm{GL}_2$-action on a sheaf over the projective line, and read off the Banach representation.
proofs.scope: An outline of Colmez's construction and classification for $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ and irreducible $V$. Reducible $V$ and the compatibility with the classical and mod $p$ correspondences are not covered, and no other group or base field has a known correspondence.

roles.why: Only for $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ does the mirabolic action on $D(V)$ extend to the whole group.
A finite extension $L$ gives a $p$-adic Banach space setting where unitary completions and reduction modulo $p$ exist.
A [p-adic representation](c:p-adic-representation) that is absolutely [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation) gives an irreducible $\Pi(V)$ and a non-ordinary one.

steps.slogan: Attach to $V$ its étale [(φ,Γ)-module](c:phi-gamma-module) $D(V)$.
steps.detail: Fontaine's equivalence identifies continuous representations of $G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$ on finite $L$-vector spaces with étale $(\varphi,\Gamma)$-modules. The module $D=D(V)$ has rank 2, and the mirabolic subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ acts on it through $\varphi$, $\Gamma$ and multiplication by $(1+T)^b$ (Colmez).

steps.slogan: Extend the mirabolic action to $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ on a sheaf $D\boxtimes\mathbb{P}^1$.
steps.detail: Colmez defines an involution $w_D$ that, with the mirabolic action, gives an action of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ on sections over $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{Q}_p)$; $D$ is the space of sections over $\mathbb{Z}_p$. He builds $w_D$ first for trianguline $D$ by explicit formulas and then extends it to every $D$ by an approximation argument.

steps.slogan: Take the unitary [Banach](c:banach-space) quotient of $D\boxtimes\mathbb{P}^1$ as $\Pi(V)$.
steps.detail: Colmez shows that $D\boxtimes\mathbb{P}^1$ sits in an exact sequence $0\to\Pi(V)^*\otimes\delta\to D\boxtimes\mathbb{P}^1\to\Pi(V)\to0$ with $\delta$ a character. The quotient $\Pi(V)$ is a unitary Banach representation of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$.

steps.slogan: Prove that $\Pi(V)$ is admissible and topologically irreducible.
steps.detail: Colmez controls the reduction modulo $p$ of $\Pi(V)$ with Breuil's mod $p$ correspondence (Berger and Breuil for crystalline $V$). This gives admissibility, and irreducibility of $\Pi(V)$ when $V$ is irreducible.

steps.slogan: Recover $V$ from $\Pi(V)$ with the Montréal functor and classify the non-ordinary representations.
steps.detail: Colmez's functor $\mathbf V$ applied to $\Pi(V)$ returns $V$, which gives injectivity of $V\mapsto\Pi(V)$. He also shows that every absolutely irreducible non-ordinary unitary admissible Banach representation $\Pi$ equals $\Pi(\mathbf V(\Pi))$, which gives surjectivity.

concepts.c:galois-representation: The Galois side of the correspondence consists of these representations.
concepts.c:p-adic-representation: The representation $V$ over $L$ is the input of the whole construction.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Irreducibility of $V$ matches irreducible, non-ordinary Banach representations.
concepts.c:phi-gamma-module: The module $D(V)$ carries the Borel action that Colmez extends.
concepts.c:banach-space: The target of the correspondence is a unitary Banach representation.

source.ref: P. Colmez, Représentations de GL2(Qp) et (φ,Γ)-modules, Astérisque 330 (2010), 281-509
source.note: Colmez constructs Pi(V) and proves its properties. Berger and Breuil (Sur quelques représentations potentiellement cristallines de GL2(Qp), Asterisque 330) supply the link with the mod p correspondence; Paskunas (The image of Colmez's Montreal functor, Publ. Math. IHES 118, 2013) gives another proof of the classification.

statement: Let $K$ be an ordered field and $A$, $B$, $C$ points of the plane $K^2$. If a line $\ell$ contains none of $A,B,C$ and meets the segment $AB$, then $\ell$ meets exactly one of the segments $AC$ and $BC$.

hypotheses.text: The plane is $K^2$ for an ordered field $K$, and [betweenness](c:betweenness) is defined by $P=X+t(Z-X)$ with $0<t<1$.
The points $A$, $B$, $C$ are not collinear.
The line $\ell$ contains none of $A$, $B$, $C$.
The line $\ell$ meets the segment $AB$.

conclusion: The line $\ell$ meets exactly one of the segments $AC$ and $BC$, at a point strictly between its ends.

proofs.name: Sign of an affine function
proofs.slogan: Write the line as the zero set of an affine function and read the crossings of segments from signs.
proofs.scope: The coordinate plane over any ordered field, the real plane included. In [Hilbert's axioms](c:hilbert-s-axioms) this statement is Pasch's axiom (axiom II.4), which Euclid's postulates do not imply; the proof shows that coordinate planes satisfy it.

roles.why: Coordinates over an ordered field make [betweenness](c:betweenness) and the sign of an affine function meaningful.
The sign argument also holds for collinear points, so non-collinearity is not needed here.
The line misses the three vertices, so $f$ is nonzero at $A$, $B$ and $C$ and has a definite sign there.
The crossing of $AB$ forces opposite signs of $f$ at $A$ and $B$.

steps.slogan: Reduce crossing a segment to a sign change of an affine function.
steps.detail: Write $\ell=\{P: f(P)=0\}$ with $f(p_1,p_2)=ap_1+bp_2+c$ and $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$. For $f(X),f(Y)\ne0$ we have $f(X+t(Y-X))=f(X)+t\,(f(Y)-f(X))$, which vanishes for some $t\in(0,1)$ exactly when $f(X)$ and $f(Y)$ have opposite signs, namely at $t=f(X)/(f(X)-f(Y))$.

steps.slogan: Get opposite signs of $f$ at $A$ and $B$ from the crossing of $AB$.
steps.detail: The line $\ell$ meets $AB$, and $f(A),f(B)\ne0$ because $A,B\notin\ell$. By step 1, $f(A)f(B)<0$.

steps.slogan: Compare the sign of $f(C)$ with the signs at $A$ and $B$.
steps.detail: Since $C\notin\ell$, we have $f(C)\ne0$. The values $f(A)$ and $f(B)$ have opposite signs, so $f(C)$ has the sign of exactly one of them.

steps.slogan: Read off the crossed side from the sign of $f(C)$.
steps.detail: If $f(C)$ has the sign of $f(A)$, then $f(B)f(C)<0$ and $f(A)f(C)>0$. By step 1, $\ell$ meets $BC$ strictly between $B$ and $C$ and misses $AC$. The other case is symmetric and gives $AC$.

concepts.c:betweenness: Betweenness defines segments, so crossing a segment means an interior point.
concepts.c:hilbert-s-axioms: Pasch's statement is an order axiom in this axiom system.

source.note: The standard check that a coordinate plane over an ordered field satisfies Pasch's axiom, as in textbook treatments of Hilbert's order axioms.

statement: In a [circle](c:circle) of radius $R$, the sides $a_5$, $a_6$, $a_{10}$ of the inscribed regular pentagon, hexagon and decagon satisfy $a_5^2=a_6^2+a_{10}^2$. So the three sides form a right triangle.

hypotheses.text: A [circle](c:circle) has radius $R>0$.
The [regular polygons](c:regular-polygon) with 5, 6 and 10 sides are inscribed in this circle and have sides $a_5$, $a_6$, $a_{10}$.

conclusion: The sides satisfy $a_5^2=a_6^2+a_{10}^2$, so by the converse of the Pythagorean theorem they form a right triangle.

proofs.name: Chord lengths and the golden relation
proofs.slogan: Write the three sides as chords, show that the decagon side solves $d^2+d-1=0$, and add squares.
proofs.scope: Any radius, by scaling to $R=1$. The proof is trigonometric; Euclid's own proof (Elements XIII.10) uses the golden section instead.

roles.why: Scaling the [circle](c:circle) to radius 1 reduces the claim to three explicit chord lengths.
A side of a [regular polygon](c:regular-polygon) with $n$ sides is a chord of central angle $2\pi/n$.

steps.slogan: Express each side as a chord of the unit circle.
steps.detail: With $R=1$, the side of the regular $n$-gon is the [chord](c:chord) of central angle $2\pi/n$, so $a_n=2\sin(\pi/n)$. Hence $a_6=2\sin30^\circ=1$, $a_{10}=2\sin18^\circ=:d$ and $a_5=2\sin36^\circ$.

steps.slogan: Show that $d$ satisfies $d^2+d-1=0$.
steps.detail: For $\theta=18^\circ$ we have $2\theta+3\theta=90^\circ$, so $\sin2\theta=\cos3\theta$. This gives $2\sin\theta\cos\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta$, hence $2\sin\theta=1-4\sin^2\theta$ after dividing by $\cos\theta\ne0$ and using $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$. With $d=2\sin\theta$ this reads $d=1-d^2$.

steps.slogan: Express $a_5^2$ through $d$.
steps.detail: Since $\cos2x=1-2\sin^2x$ by the Pythagorean identity $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$, we get $a_5^2=4\sin^236^\circ=2-2\cos72^\circ$. Because $\cos72^\circ=\sin18^\circ=d/2$, this gives $a_5^2=2-d$.

steps.slogan: Add the squares of the hexagon side and the decagon side.
steps.detail: By step 2, $d^2=1-d$, so $a_6^2+a_{10}^2=1+d^2=2-d$. By step 3, this equals $a_5^2$.

steps.slogan: Read the identity as a right triangle.
steps.detail: A right triangle with legs $a_6$ and $a_{10}$ has hypotenuse $\sqrt{a_6^2+a_{10}^2}=a_5$ by the Pythagorean theorem. A triangle is determined by its three sides, so every triangle with sides $a_5,a_6,a_{10}$ is this right triangle.

concepts.c:circle: The sides are chords of a circle of fixed radius.
concepts.c:regular-polygon: The three polygons have equal sides and central angles $2\pi/n$.
concepts.c:chord: A side of an inscribed polygon is a chord with a computable length.

source.note: A trigonometric proof of Euclid, Elements XIII.10.

statement: Let $\Omega$ be a bounded simply connected planar domain and $\Omega^*$ the disc of the same area. Then the [torsional rigidity](c:torsion) of $\Omega$ is at most that of $\Omega^*$. The rigidity is a fixed positive multiple of $T(\Omega)=\sup_{v\in H^1_0(\Omega)\setminus\{0\}}\big(\int_\Omega v\big)^2\big/\int_\Omega|\nabla v|^2$.

hypotheses.text: The cross section $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ is a bounded simply connected domain, so its [torsional rigidity](c:torsion) is a fixed positive multiple of $T(\Omega)$.
The disc $\Omega^*$ has the same area as $\Omega$.

conclusion: $T(\Omega)\le T(\Omega^*)$, so the disc has the largest torsional rigidity among cross sections of that area.

proofs.name: Polya's symmetrization
proofs.slogan: Replace a test function by its symmetrization on the disc, which keeps its integral and lowers its energy, so the torsion quotient grows.
proofs.scope: The inequality holds for every bounded open set; simple connectivity matters only for the identification of the rigidity with $T(\Omega)$. The equality case, that only discs attain the maximum, is not proved here.

roles.why: For a simply connected section the [torsional rigidity](c:torsion) is a multiple of the Dirichlet quantity $T(\Omega)$.
Equal area makes the symmetrized function a competitor on $\Omega^*$ with the same integral.

steps.slogan: Write the torsion functional $T(\Omega)$ as a maximum of Rayleigh quotients.
steps.detail:
Let $u$ in the [Sobolev space](c:sobolev-space) $H^1_0(\Omega)$ solve $-\Delta u=1$. For $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, $\int v=\int
abla u\cdot
abla v\le\|
abla u\|\,\|
abla v\|$ by Cauchy-Schwarz, so $(\int v)^2/\int|
abla v|^2\le\int|
abla u|^2=\int u$, with equality for $v=u$. Hence $T(\Omega)=\int u$.

steps.slogan: Replace $v\ge0$ by its Schwarz symmetrization $v^*$ on $\Omega^*$.
steps.detail: Replacing $v$ by $|v|$ keeps $\int|\nabla v|^2$ and does not decrease $|\int v|$, so take $v\ge0$. The function $v^*$ is radial, decreasing in $|x|$ and supported in $\Omega^*$, and $|\{v^*>t\}|=|\{v>t\}|$ for all $t$, so $\int v^*=\int v$.

steps.slogan: Show that symmetrization does not increase the Dirichlet integral.
steps.detail:
By the coarea formula and Cauchy-Schwarz, $\int|
abla v|^2\ge\int_0^\infty 4\pi\mu(t)/(-\mu'(t))\,dt$ with $\mu(t)=|\{v>t\}|$, because each level set has perimeter at least $2\sqrt{\pi\mu(t)}$ by the isoperimetric inequality. The level sets of $v^*$ are circles, so equality holds for $v^*$ and $\int|
abla v^*|^2\le\int|
abla v|^2$.

steps.slogan: Compare the quotients of $v$ and $v^*$ and take the supremum over $v$.
steps.detail:
For $v
e0$, $(\int v)^2/\int|
abla v|^2\le(\int v^*)^2/\int|
abla v^*|^2\le T(\Omega^*)$, because $v^*\in H^1_0(\Omega^*)$ is an admissible test function. The supremum over $v$ gives $T(\Omega)\le T(\Omega^*)$.

concepts.c:torsion: Torsional rigidity measures resistance to twisting and equals $T(\Omega)$ up to a constant.
concepts.c:sobolev-space: The test functions lie in $H^1_0$, where the Dirichlet energy is finite.

source.note: G. Polya, Torsional rigidity, principal frequency, electrostatic capacity and symmetrization, Quarterly of Applied Mathematics 6 (1948), 267-277; also Polya and Szego, Isoperimetric Inequalities in Mathematical Physics (1951).

statement: Let $K$ be a complete non-archimedean valued field with valuation ring $\mathcal{O}$ and $f=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$ a [power series](c:p-adic-power-series) over $K$ with $a_n\to0$ and not all $a_n$ zero. Let $N$ be the largest index with $|a_N|=\max_n|a_n|$. Then $f$ has at most $N$ zeros in $\mathcal{O}$.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is complete for a non-archimedean [absolute value](c:absolute-value), with valuation ring $\mathcal{O}=\{x:|x|\le1\}$.
The coefficients satisfy $a_n\to0$, so the series converges on $\mathcal{O}$.
Not all coefficients $a_n$ are zero.

conclusion: The series $f$ has at most $N$ zeros in $\mathcal{O}$, counted without multiplicity.

proofs.name: Induction on the last maximal index
proofs.slogan: Divide out a zero by factoring $f(x)-f(\alpha)$ and induct on the index of the last maximal coefficient.
proofs.scope: Zeros in $\mathcal{O}$ are counted without multiplicity, and for $N=0$ there are none. The index $N$ is the abscissa of the right end of the lowest edge of the [Newton polygon](c:newton-polygon) of $f$, which counts the zeros over an algebraic closure.

roles.why: Completeness makes the rearrangement of the double series valid, and the ultrametric inequality drives every estimate of an [absolute value](c:absolute-value).
Coefficients tending to $0$ make the series converge on $\mathcal{O}$ and make the maximum of $|a_n|$ exist.
A nonzero series has a maximal coefficient, so the index $N$ is defined.

steps.slogan: Treat the case $N=0$ directly.
steps.detail: If $N=0$, then $|a_n|<|a_0|$ for $n\ge1$. For $x\in\mathcal{O}$ the ultrametric inequality gives $|f(x)-a_0|\le\max_{n\ge1}|a_n|<|a_0|$, so $|f(x)|=|a_0|\ne0$ and $f$ has no zero in $\mathcal{O}$.

steps.slogan: Factor out a zero $\alpha\in\mathcal{O}$ of $f$ as $f(x)=(x-\alpha)g(x)$.
steps.detail: Let $N\ge1$ and $f(\alpha)=0$ with $\alpha\in\mathcal{O}$. Then $f(x)=f(x)-f(\alpha)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n(x^n-\alpha^n)=(x-\alpha)\sum_{j\ge0}b_jx^j$ with $b_j=\sum_{n>j}a_n\alpha^{n-1-j}$; the rearrangement is valid because all terms tend to $0$ in a complete field.

steps.slogan: Show that $g$ has last maximal index $N-1$.
steps.detail: Put $M=|a_N|$. Every $b_j$ has $|b_j|\le\max_{n>j}|a_n|\le M$ because $|\alpha|\le1$, with $|b_j|<M$ for $j\ge N$ and $|b_{N-1}|=|a_N|=M$ because $|a_n|<M$ for $n>N$. So $b_j\to0$ and $N-1$ is the last index of the maximal coefficient of $g$.

steps.slogan: Apply the induction hypothesis to $g$ and count the zeros of $f$.
steps.detail: By induction on $N$, $g$ has at most $N-1$ zeros in $\mathcal{O}$. Since $K$ has no zero divisors, every zero $\beta\ne\alpha$ of $f$ in $\mathcal{O}$ is a zero of $g$. Hence $f$ has at most $1+(N-1)=N$ zeros in $\mathcal{O}$.

concepts.c:p-adic-power-series: The statement and the factorization concern series with coefficients tending to zero.
concepts.c:absolute-value: The ultrametric inequality controls every estimate of coefficients and values.
concepts.c:newton-polygon: The Newton polygon gives the same count of zeros over an algebraic closure.

source.note: The classical induction proof, as in Koblitz, p-adic Numbers, p-adic Analysis, and Zeta-Functions, 2nd edition, Chapter IV, section 4 (Strassmann's theorem).

statement: Let $H$ be a finite [hypergraph](c:hypergraph) on $n$ vertices whose edges have at least 2 vertices and whose automorphism group is [transitive](c:transitive-group) on the vertices. If $\alpha$ is the independence number of $H$, then the [chromatic number](c:chromatic-number) satisfies $\chi(H)\le\big\lceil\frac n\alpha(1+\ln\alpha)\big\rceil\le\big\lceil\frac n\alpha(1+\ln n)\big\rceil$.

hypotheses.text: The [hypergraph](c:hypergraph) $H=(V,E)$ is finite with $|V|=n$, and every edge has at least 2 vertices.
The automorphism group $\Gamma$ of $H$ is [transitive](c:transitive-group) on $V$.
The number $\alpha$ is the largest size of an [independent set](c:independent-set), a vertex set that contains no edge.

proofs.name: Random translates of a maximum independent set
proofs.slogan: Cover the vertices by random automorphic images of a maximum independent set, then give each leftover vertex its own color.
proofs.scope: Every finite hypergraph with a transitive automorphism group and edges of size at least 2; for $\alpha=1$ the bound is $n$. The argument is a probabilistic covering argument of Lovász type.

roles.why: Finiteness of $H$ and of $\Gamma$ gives a uniform random automorphism, and edges of size at least 2 make single vertices independent.
[Transitivity](c:transitive-group) makes the chance of covering a vertex the same for every vertex.
A maximum [independent set](c:independent-set) of size $\alpha$ gives the covering probability $\alpha/n$ and the count of colors.

steps.slogan: Show that a random automorphic image of an independent set covers each vertex with probability $\alpha/n$.
steps.detail: Let $I$ be an independent set of size $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ a uniform random element of $\Gamma$. By transitivity, $|\{\sigma:\sigma(u)=v\}|=|\Gamma|/n$ for all $u,v$, so $\Pr[v\in\sigma(I)]=|I|/n=\alpha/n$. Every image $\sigma(I)$ is again independent.

steps.slogan: Choose $k$ independent images whose union leaves few vertices uncovered.
steps.detail: Take $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_k$ independent and uniform. A vertex stays uncovered with probability $(1-\alpha/n)^k\le e^{-k\alpha/n}$. With $k=\lceil(n/\alpha)\ln\alpha\rceil$ the expected number of uncovered vertices is at most $n/\alpha$, so some choice leaves $u\le n/\alpha$ vertices uncovered.

steps.slogan: Color the images, then color each leftover vertex with its own color.
steps.detail: Give the vertices of $\sigma_i(I)$ that are not in earlier images color $i$, and give each of the $u$ uncovered vertices a new color. A subset of an independent set is independent, and a single vertex is independent, so no edge is monochromatic and the coloring uses $k+u$ colors.

steps.slogan: Bound the number of colors by the claimed expression.
steps.detail: We have $k+u\le\lceil(n/\alpha)\ln\alpha\rceil+\lfloor n/\alpha\rfloor\le\lceil(n/\alpha)(1+\ln\alpha)\rceil$, because $\lceil a\rceil+\lfloor b\rfloor\le\lceil a+b\rceil$. Since $\alpha\le n$, this is at most $\lceil(n/\alpha)(1+\ln n)\rceil$.

concepts.c:hypergraph: Edges may have more than two vertices, so a coloring must avoid monochromatic edges.
concepts.c:transitive-group: Transitivity gives every vertex the same covering probability.
concepts.c:chromatic-number: The chromatic number is the least number of independent classes that cover the vertices.
concepts.c:independent-set: Color classes are independent sets, and images of an independent set stay independent.

source.note: The probabilistic covering argument of L. Lovász, On the ratio of optimal integral and fractional covers, Discrete Mathematics 13 (1975), 383-390, applied to the images of a maximum independent set.

statement: The [Kontsevich integral](c:kontsevich-integral) $Z$ of the unknot has, in the space $\mathcal{B}$ of [Jacobi diagrams](c:jacobi-diagram) (identified with the diagram algebra of the circle by the PBW map $\chi$), the value $\chi^{-1}Z(\text{unknot})=\exp\big(\sum_{n\ge1}b_{2n}\omega_{2n}\big)$. Here $\omega_{2n}$ is the wheel with $2n$ legs, and $\sum_n b_{2n}x^{2n}=\frac12\log\frac{\sinh(x/2)}{x/2}$ defines the [modified Bernoulli numbers](c:modified-bernoulli-number).

hypotheses.text: The knot is the unknot with framing 0.
The invariant $Z$ is the Kontsevich integral, the universal [Vassiliev invariant](c:vassiliev-invariant) with values in the completed algebra of [Jacobi diagrams](c:jacobi-diagram).

conclusion: The unknot's Kontsevich integral is the exponential of a series of wheels whose coefficients are the modified Bernoulli numbers $b_{2n}$.

proofs.name: Cabling and the Hopf link
proofs.slogan: Compute the Kontsevich integral of cables of the unknot in two ways, untangle the equations with the Hopf-link Wheeling map, and solve for the wheel coefficients.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof of the Wheels conjecture, which proves it together with the Wheeling conjecture; the case of Lie algebras was proved earlier by Bar-Natan, Garoufalidis, Rozansky and Thurston.

roles.why: The $n$-fold connected cable of the unknot is again an unknot, which gives the equations for $Z(\text{unknot})$.
The values of $Z$ in the algebra of [Jacobi diagrams](c:jacobi-diagram) are the objects that the equations determine.

steps.slogan: Place the Kontsevich integral of the unknot in the space of Jacobi diagrams.
steps.detail: The Kontsevich integral $Z$ takes values in the completed algebra $\mathcal{A}(\bigcirc)$ of [Jacobi diagrams](c:jacobi-diagram) on a circle. The PBW map $\chi\colon\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{A}(\bigcirc)$ identifies it with the space $\mathcal{B}$ of diagrams with unordered legs, and one asks for $\chi^{-1}Z(\text{unknot})$.

steps.slogan: Compare the Kontsevich integrals of cables of the unknot with that of the unknot.
steps.detail: The connected $n$-fold cable of the unknot is again an unknot. Computing its Kontsevich integral directly and through the cabling formula gives equations that relate $Z(\text{unknot})$ to its images under the coproduct.

steps.slogan: Express the Wheeling map by the Kontsevich integral of a cut Hopf link.
steps.detail: The Kontsevich integral of a [Hopf link](c:hopf-link) with one component cut open, a bead on a wire, defines the Wheeling map. This map is an algebra isomorphism between the two natural products on $\mathcal{B}$, so it converts the cabling equations into equations in one algebra.

steps.slogan: Solve the cabling equations for the logarithm of $\chi^{-1}Z(\text{unknot})$.
steps.detail: The equations force $\log\chi^{-1}Z(\text{unknot})$ to be a series of wheels $\sum_nc_{2n}\omega_{2n}$ with scalar coefficients $c_{2n}$, and they determine these coefficients.

steps.slogan: Identify the wheel coefficients as the modified Bernoulli numbers.
steps.detail: The solution has $c_{2n}=b_{2n}$, where $\sum_nb_{2n}x^{2n}=\frac12\log\frac{\sinh(x/2)}{x/2}$ is the generating series of the [modified Bernoulli numbers](c:modified-bernoulli-number). Exponentiating gives the theorem.

concepts.c:kontsevich-integral: The theorem computes this invariant for the unknot.
concepts.c:jacobi-diagram: Wheels are Jacobi diagrams, and the value of $Z$ lives in their algebra.
concepts.c:vassiliev-invariant: The Kontsevich integral is the universal Vassiliev invariant, which carries all finite type invariants.
concepts.c:modified-bernoulli-number: These numbers are the coefficients of the wheels.
concepts.c:hopf-link: A cut Hopf link gives the Wheeling map used to solve the equations.

source.ref: D. Bar-Natan, T. Q. T. Le and D. P. Thurston, Two applications of elementary knot theory to Lie algebras and Vassiliev invariants, Geometry & Topology 7 (2003), 1-31
source.note: This paper proves the Wheels and Wheeling conjectures of Bar-Natan, Garoufalidis, Rozansky and Thurston (Wheels, wheeling, and the Kontsevich integral of the unknot, Israel J. Math. 119, 2000), who proved them for Lie algebras.

statement: The theory of the real [exponential field](c:exponential-field) $(\mathbb{R},+,\cdot,<,0,1,\exp)$ is model complete. Equivalently, every definable set is the projection of the zero set of finitely many terms built from the field operations and $\exp$, an exponential variety.

hypotheses.text: The structure is the ordered field $\mathbb{R}$ with the function $\exp$ and no other function.

conclusion: Every set definable in $\mathbb{R}_{\exp}$ is existentially definable, that is, a projection of an exponential variety.

proofs.name: Theorem of the complement for Pfaffian sets
proofs.slogan: Show that complements of projections of exponential varieties are again such projections, then eliminate negations from formulas by induction.
proofs.scope: The theorem for $\mathbb{R}_{\exp}$; Wilkie also proves it for the field with all restricted Pfaffian functions. With Khovanskii's finiteness theorem it makes $\mathbb{R}_{\exp}$ [o-minimal](c:o-minimal-structure), which is not proved here.

roles.why: The structure is the [exponential field](c:exponential-field) whose function $\exp$ is Pfaffian, so Khovanskii's bounds and Wilkie's complement theorem apply.

steps.slogan: Cast the exponential function as a Pfaffian function with finiteness bounds.
steps.detail: The function $\exp$ satisfies $y'=y$, so it forms a Pfaffian chain of length 1. Khovanskii's theory bounds the number of connected components of zero sets of Pfaffian functions in terms of their format, which supplies the finiteness that the argument needs.

steps.slogan: Prove the theorem of the complement for projections of restricted Pfaffian varieties.
steps.detail: Wilkie shows that the complement of a projection of a restricted Pfaffian variety is again such a projection. This is the technical heart of the paper, and it rests on Khovanskii's bounds on the number of components.

steps.slogan: Extend the complement theorem to exponential varieties over all of $\mathbb{R}$.
steps.detail: Wilkie then treats $\exp$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$ by the same method and shows that the complement of a projection of an exponential variety is again a projection of one.

steps.slogan: Show by induction on formulas that every formula is equivalent to an existential one.
steps.detail: Existential formulas are closed under conjunction and under $\exists$, and by step 3 under the negation of an $\exists$-formula. Hence every formula, built by $\neg$, $\wedge$ and $\exists$ from atomic ones, is existential; without $\exp$ this is the Tarski-Seidenberg theorem. This is model completeness.

concepts.c:exponential-field: The theorem is about the definable sets of this structure.
concepts.c:o-minimal-structure: Model completeness with Khovanskii's bounds makes the structure o-minimal.

source.ref: A. J. Wilkie, Model completeness results for expansions of the ordered field of real numbers by restricted Pfaffian functions and the exponential function, Journal of the American Mathematical Society 9 (1996), 1051-1094
source.note: Wilkie proves a theorem of the complement for Pfaffian sets with Khovanskii's finiteness bounds and derives model completeness of the real exponential field.

statement: Let $Q\colon\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$, $U\colon\mathcal A\to\mathcal C$, $V\colon\mathcal B\to\mathcal D$, $R\colon\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ be functors with $VQ\cong RU$. Let $V$ be [monadic](c:monad), let $U$ have a left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor), and let $\mathcal A$ have [coequalizers](c:coequalizer) of reflexive pairs. If $R$ has a left adjoint, then $Q$ has a left adjoint.

hypotheses.text: The square commutes up to natural isomorphism: $V\circ Q\cong R\circ U$.
The functor $V$ is [monadic](c:monad).
The functor $U$ has a left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor).
The category $\mathcal A$ has [coequalizers](c:coequalizer) of reflexive pairs.
The functor $R$ has a left adjoint.

formal.difference: The declaration states the same theorem with the square commuting up to natural isomorphism and the hypotheses given as typeclass assumptions on $U$, $R$ and $V$. Its conclusion Q.IsRightAdjoint says that $Q$ has a left adjoint.

proofs.name: Adjoint triangle theorem
proofs.slogan: Build the left adjoint of $Q$ as a reflexive coequalizer of images of free objects, using that every object of $\mathcal B$ is a coequalizer of free objects.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The proof first builds a left adjoint $F'$ of $V\circ Q$ and then lifts it through the monadic functor $V$, which is the adjoint triangle theorem.

roles.why: The isomorphism $V\circ Q\cong R\circ U$ transfers the left adjoint of $R\circ U$ to $V\circ Q$.
[Monadicity](c:monad) of $V$ presents every object of $\mathcal B$ as a coequalizer of free objects.
The left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) of $U$ is one factor of the left adjoint of $R\circ U$.
Reflexive [coequalizers](c:coequalizer) in $\mathcal A$ define the object part of the new left adjoint.
The left adjoint of $R$ is the other factor of the left adjoint of $R\circ U$.

steps.slogan: Show that $V\circ Q$ has a left adjoint $F'$.
steps.detail: A composite of functors with left adjoints has a left adjoint, so $R\circ U$ has one, namely $F'=F_U\circ L$ with $L\dashv R$ and $F_U\dashv U$. The natural isomorphism $V\circ Q\cong R\circ U$ transfers the adjunction $F'\dashv V\circ Q$.

steps.slogan: Write each object of $\mathcal B$ as a coequalizer of free objects.
steps.detail: Let $F\dashv V$ with counit $\varepsilon$, which exists because $V$ is [monadic](c:monad). For every $Y\in\mathcal B$, $Y$ is the [coequalizer](c:coequalizer) of $FV\varepsilon_Y$ and $\varepsilon_{FVY}$ (Beck's coequalizer), so $\varepsilon_Y$ is a regular epimorphism.

steps.slogan: Define $LY$ as a reflexive coequalizer in $\mathcal A$.
steps.detail: Let $LY$ be the coequalizer of $F'V\varepsilon_Y$ and $o_Y=\delta_{F'VY}\circ F'V(\varepsilon_{QF'VY}\circ F\iota_{VY})$, where $\iota,\delta$ are the unit and counit of $F'\dashv VQ$. Both maps have the common section $F'\eta_{VY}$, so they are a reflexive pair and the coequalizer exists.

steps.slogan: Show that maps out of $LY$ correspond to maps $Y\to QA$.
steps.detail: A map $LY\to A$ is a map $f\colon F'VY\to A$ with $f\circ F'V\varepsilon_Y=f\circ o_Y$. Under $F'\dashv VQ$ it corresponds to $g\colon VY\to VQA$, and under $F\dashv V$ the equation says that the adjoint $FVY\to QA$ of $g$ coequalizes $FV\varepsilon_Y$ and $\varepsilon_{FVY}$. By step 2 such maps are exactly the maps $Y\to QA$.

steps.slogan: Make $L$ a functor and conclude that it is left adjoint to $Q$.
steps.detail: The bijections $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(LY,A)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal B}(Y,QA)$ are natural in $A$ and in $Y$. A family of natural bijections of this kind defines a functor $L\colon\mathcal B\to\mathcal A$ with $L\dashv Q$.

concepts.c:adjoint-functor: The theorem builds a left adjoint, and every step moves along adjunctions.
concepts.c:monad: Monadicity of $V$ gives the presentation of objects by free objects.
concepts.c:coequalizer: Reflexive coequalizers define the object part of the new left adjoint.

source.note: mathlib reduces the theorem to the adjoint triangle theorem isRightAdjoint_triangle_lift_monadic. Its construction LiftLeftAdjoint.constructLeftAdjoint takes the reflexive coequalizer of step 3, and Monad.beckAlgebraCoequalizer gives the Beck coequalizer of step 2.

statement: Let $K$ be a totally imaginary [number field](c:number-field), $U$ a nonempty open subscheme of $\mathrm{Spec}$ of its [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers), and $F$ a [constructible sheaf](c:constructible-sheaf) on $U$ with finite stalks. Then $H^r_c(U,F)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^{3-r}_U(F,\mathbb{G}_m)$ are finite, and the Yoneda pairing into $H^3_c(U,\mathbb{G}_m)\cong\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is perfect for every $r$.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field) with no real place, and $U$ is a nonempty open subscheme of $\mathrm{Spec}$ of its [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers).
The sheaf $F$ is a [constructible sheaf](c:constructible-sheaf) of abelian groups on the étale site of $U$ with finite stalks.

conclusion: For every integer $r$, the Yoneda pairing $\mathrm{Ext}^{3-r}_U(F,\mathbb{G}_m)\times H^r_c(U,F)\to H^3_c(U,\mathbb{G}_m)\cong\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is a perfect pairing of finite groups.

proofs.name: Class field theory and Poitou-Tate duality
proofs.slogan: Compute the cohomology of the multiplicative group by class field theory, reduce constructible sheaves to locally constant ones and points, and use Poitou-Tate duality.
proofs.scope: An outline for a totally imaginary $K$; for a field with a real place the pairing is perfect away from 2-torsion. Constructible sheaves with finite stalks are torsion.

roles.why: A [number field](c:number-field) with no real place gives the trace isomorphism $H^3_c(U,\mathbb{G}_m)\cong\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ from class field theory.
Constructibility lets the sheaf be cut into locally constant pieces and sheaves at closed points, and finite stalks make the groups finite.

steps.slogan: Compute $H^3_c(U,\mathbb{G}_m)$ and its trace map to $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ by class field theory.
steps.detail: The exact sequence $0\to\mathrm{Br}(K)\to\bigoplus_v\mathrm{Br}(K_v)\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\to0$ of [Brauer groups](c:brauer-group) holds by the Hasse principle and the reciprocity law. With $H^r(K_v,\mathbb{G}_m)=0$ for $r\ge3$ it gives $H^3_c(U,\mathbb{G}_m)\cong\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ and defines the pairing.

steps.slogan: Reduce constructible sheaves to locally constant sheaves and sheaves at points.
steps.detail: Shrinking $U$ makes $F$ locally constant on an open $V\subset U$, and $0\to j_!j^*F\to F\to i_*i^*F\to0$ is exact, with $i$ the inclusion of finitely many closed points. Both sides of the duality are cohomological functors in $F$, so the five lemma reduces the claim to $j_!$ of a locally constant sheaf and to sheaves at closed points.

steps.slogan: Prove the case of a sheaf supported at a closed point by duality over the finite residue field.
steps.detail: At a closed point $x$, the local cohomology of $\mathbb{G}_m$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ in degree 1 and zero otherwise, so $\mathrm{Ext}_U(i_*M,\mathbb{G}_m)$ becomes $\mathrm{Ext}_{k(x)}(M,\mathbb{Z})$ with a shift of 1. The pairing is then the duality of Galois cohomology of the finite field $k(x)$.

steps.slogan: Prove the locally constant case of invertible order by Poitou-Tate duality.
steps.detail: Shrink $V$ until the order $n$ of $F$ is invertible on $V$. The groups are finite by the finiteness theorems of number theory, and the pairing is perfect by comparing the long exact sequence of compact-support cohomology with the Poitou-Tate sequence of [Galois cohomology](c:galois-cohomology) for the dual sheaf $\mathrm{Hom}(F,\mu_n)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the cases by the five lemma.
steps.detail: The maps $H^r_c(U,F)\to\mathrm{Ext}^{3-r}_U(F,\mathbb{G}_m)^\vee$ form a morphism of cohomological functors in $F$. It is an isomorphism for pieces $j_!G$ and $i_*M$, so by the five lemma it is an isomorphism for every constructible $F$ with finite stalks.

concepts.c:number-field: The ring of integers of a number field is the base of the duality.
concepts.c:ring-of-integers: Its spectrum behaves like a three-dimensional object for étale cohomology.
concepts.c:constructible-sheaf: Constructible sheaves are the coefficients; they split into locally constant pieces and points.
concepts.c:brauer-group: Brauer groups carry the class field theory that gives the trace isomorphism.
concepts.c:galois-cohomology: Poitou-Tate duality for Galois cohomology gives the locally constant case.

source.ref: J. S. Milne, Arithmetic Duality Theorems, 2nd edition, BookSurge, 2006, Chapter II, Section 3
source.note: Milne proves the Artin-Verdier theorem for constructible sheaves on an open subscheme of the spectrum of a ring of integers, including the treatment of real places.
